CITY OF AVALON PLANNING COMMISSION AGENDA
  City Hall Council Chambers ∙ 410 Avalon Canyon Road, Avalon, CA
  Regular Meeting – August 28, 2024 at 5:00 p.m.

This meeting is viewable in person at the Council Chambers or via livestream:

  Facebook: (http://www.facebook.com/CityOfAvalonOfficial)
  YouTube (http://www.youtube.com/cityofavalonca)
  Website (http://www.cityofavalon.com/meetings)
  Cable (Catalina Broadband Solutions Channel 3)

The Council Chambers can accommodate a maximum of 30 participants, at which point the general
public may address the Planning Commission on an agenda item by waiting in the City Hall Court
Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time. No one will be admitted into the Council Chambers
who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. The Planning Commission is not accepting live
comments electronically at this time.

The public can submit written comments prior to 12:00 p.m. 3 days prior to the meeting in person
to the Planning Department at City Hall or via email to dromo@cityofavalon.com.

Staff reports for each agenda item are posted a minimum of 72 hours prior to the meeting and are
available for review in person or on the City website at http://www.cityofavalon.com.

 In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this
 meeting, please contact Gabrielle Morones, City Clerk’s office (310) 510-0220 ext. 119. Notification 48
 hours prior to the meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to
 this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-35.104 ADA Title II). All public records relating to an agenda item on this
 agenda are available for the public inspection at the time the records are distributed to all, or a majority of
 all, members of the Planning Commission. Such records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon

CALL TO ORDER

PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE/ROLL CALL

ORAL COMMUNICATION: This is the time for any member of the public to address the
Planning Commission on any matter not on the agenda that is within the subject matter jurisdiction
of the City. The Brown Act, with limited exceptions, does not allow the Commission or staff to
discuss or take action on issues brought forth under Public Comment. Concerns may be referred
to staff or placed on the next available agenda. Please note that comments from the public will
also be taken on each agenda item. Comments shall be limited to three minutes per person.

Anyone may appeal any decision made by the Commission to the City Council. To appeal, you

   AVALON PLANNING COMMISSION
  STAFF REPORT – PC# 2842
  Wednesday, August 28, 2024

  Application File: CUP, VAR, SPR, CDP
Item No.  – Public Hearing  Submitted by: Kelly Ribuffo, Contract Planner

A Public Hearing considering a Conditional Use Permit, Variance, Site Plan, and Coastal
Development Permit to allow the demolition of a vacant three-story apartment building and
construction of a new four-story hotel with employee housing in the Special Commercial (SC)
zone. The Proposed Project is categorically exempt from the California Environmental Quality
Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15332 (In-Fill Development Projects). The Project Site
is located within the non-appealable area of the Coastal Zone.

  Applicant:  Hamilton Pacific LLC
  Owner:  The Cameron Family Limited Partnership, Roger and Kathleen
  Wesley Living Trust dated November 21, 2019, and Suzanne T.
  Coe
  Files:  CUP, VAR, SPR, CDP
  Location of Project: 301 Beacon Street
  APN:  7480-031-040
  PC #:  2842
  File Date:  4/24/2023
  General Plan:  Special Commercial (SC)
  Zone:  Special Commercial (SC)

  BACKGROUND

  1
65059.00002\42583158.2
   Project Vicinity

  (SC)  (SC)

Existing Site:

The project site is located on a regularly shaped parcel at 301 Beacon Street. The parcel is situated
on the southeast corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street. Metropole Avenue slopes steeply
southeasterly to northeasterly from Tremont Street (south) toward Beacon Street (north). Beacon
Street slopes northwesterly from Calle Del Sol (northwest) to southeasterly (Sumner Avenue).

  2
65059.00002\42583158.2
 The project site is currently developed with a three-story, ten-unit apartment building constructed
in 1923, designed in a vernacular style with elements of Mediterranean Revival. It was constructed
with some units existing below the street grade, which allows the roofline to remain flat, similar
to the neighboring buildings along Metropole Avenue which also have units below street grade
due to the street’s steep slope. Therefore, the above-ground elevation of the building is shorter
along the rear of the building at Metropole Avenue than it is along the frontage at Metropole
Avenue and Beacon Street. There is one Pepper tree at the rear of the building, and no other
vegetation on the property.

The existing building housed short-term and seasonal visitors after its construction in 1923 and
was also occupied by members of the Cameron family between approximately 1930 and 2000.
However, it has been vacant since approximately 2000 and has fallen into a state of disrepair. The
building does not meet current building code standards and significant termite damage is present.

Existing Area Context:

All abutting properties are in the Special Commercial zone and represent a mix of commercial,
institutional, and residential uses. Surrounding uses include the Avalon Community Church (236
Metropole Avenue) to the north, a vacant residential duplex (305 Beacon Street) and the Beacon
Hill Senior Apartments (309 Beacon Street) to the east, multi-family housing to the south (310
Metropole Avenue), and the Hotel St. Lauren (231 Beacon Street) to the west.

Entitlement and Permit History:

There is no known entitlement history for the project site. The existing apartment building was
constructed in 1923, prior to the requirement for a conditional use for residential structures in the
SC zone.

  PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The applicant, Hamilton Pacific, LLC, Inc proposes to demolish the existing vacant apartment
building and construct a new four-story hotel with employee housing. The building will include
37 standard hotel rooms, four employee studio units, and a rooftop deck with an elevator and a
bathroom and outdoor prep kitchen accessory structures that extends approximately 12 feet above
the parapet.

Hotel rooms will be offered for rent on a daily basis, consistent with standard hotel operations.
The rooftop bar and restaurant will be open from 7:00 AM to 10:00 PM daily and accessible to
guests and the public. The applicant shall return to the Planning Commission at a future date for
approval of a specific Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) License.

Additional information regarding the operation of the proposed business, including a site plan, are
included in Attachments 2, 3 and 4 of this report.

  3
65059.00002\42583158.2
 Construction Phasing:

The site will be developed over two phases based on the Southern California Edison (SCE) water
allotments for the property. At the time of this report, the proposed project has a water allotment
granted for an equivalent of 10 bedrooms/units. The applicant has been placed on the waitlist for
Phase II of the project, which is approximately an additional 34 bedrooms/units. The schedule for
SCE to release the additional water allocation is unknown at this time.

Phase 1

  •  Demolition of the existing apartment building, final grading, and installation of utility
  connections.
  •  Build the hotel infrastructure, exterior/architectural, install elevator to all four floors with
  rooftop access, and install all mechanical to fully support first phase.
  •  Develop first floor interior which will consist of the lobby, seven hotel rooms, one
  managers apartment, and an outdoor patio (8 water units). All hotel rooms will be double
  occupancy in accordance with the SCE water allotment standards.
  •  Develop second floor interior with one hotel room and one housekeeper suite (2 water
  units).

Safety and security measures will be built in as part of Phase 1 to protect the development until
Phase 2 construction. During Phase 1, the second-floor hotel rooms that will be fully built out will
be closest to the elevator for convenience. The hallway and doors to the unfinished rooms will be
completed but secured with locks. It is anticipated that the remaining rooms on the second floor
will be completed to rough framing, rough plumbing, rough electrical, and functional fire
sprinklers only. The elevator will be fully functional from the lobby, second floor and roof. The
elevator will be programmed such that only those with a special access key, generally held by the
on-site manager and the applicant’s construction superintendent, will be able to access the
unfinished floors three and four. Floors three and four will be developed with structural and safety
components only such as, rough framing, rough electrical, rough mechanical, rough plumbing,
fully-operable fire sprinklers, and stair access with a locked door for each unfinished floor.
Additionally, until such time as the laundry facilities are completed on floors three and four, all
laundry services will be contracted.

Phase 2

  •  Finish interior buildout of nine hotel rooms on the second floor (9 water units).
  •  Finish interior buildout of ten hotel rooms, one housekeeper apartment, one laundry room
  on the third floor (11 water units).
  •  Finish interior development 10 hotel rooms, one housekeeper apartment, one laundry room
  on the fourth floor (11 water units).
  •  Convert three rooms to four-person occupancy rooms on the first floor. These rooms are
  planned for exclusive use by applicant’s construction crew during the weekdays, and
  general hotel rooms for the weekend. (3 water units – where double occupancy per room
  counts for one water credit).

  4
65059.00002\42583158.2
   •  Install rooftop deck with operable bathrooms and cooking area, additional rooftop
  mechanical to support second phase (unknown number of water credits to be obtained).

Development Standards:

The proposed project must comply with development standards set forth in Avalon Municipal
Code (AMC) Section 9-6.304 for the SC zoning district as follows:

In addition to the development standards for the zone, the project must also comply with standards
for hotel room size per AMC Section 9-7.901, Hotel Density.

  Table 2: Development Standards – Hotel Room Size

  DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS

Issue 1: Variances from Development Standards

The applicant is requesting multiple variances from the development standards for the SC zone, as
follows:

  •  Allow building height of 28 feet to 44 feet, with an additional 10 feet for the elevator
  building and kitchen/restroom/mechanical roof structure, where 28 feet is allowed.
  •  Allow 97% lot coverage, where a maximum of 80% is allowed.
  •  Allow 383% floor area, where a maximum of 140% is allowed.

Per AMC Chapter 9-8.405, variances from development standards may be permitted by the
Planning Commission where the special circumstances may deprive a property of privileges
enjoyed by other property in the vicinity and under identical zoning classification, the property is
not granted special privileges beyond those available to similar properties, does not permit a use
that is otherwise not allowed, and complies with the Avalon Local Coastal Program.

Though the property is of regular size, the sloped topography of the lot is unusual compared to the
majority of other properties within the SC zone. The majority of lots within the Special
Commercial zone, and commercial zoning districts in general, are located within the “Flats”. As a
result, the development standards have been written to apply to lots with flat topography. For
instance, the maximum building height in the SC zone is 28 feet. The municipal code definition
for building height is “…the vertical distance from the lot's natural surface to the highest point of

  6
65059.00002\42583158.2
 the building.” (AMC Section 9-3.608). Other zones in the city, particularly the residential zones,
have additional detailed standards for measurement of building height (low slope, hillside, steep
hillside) that account for the topography present within the zone to allow for equitable
development of all lots. However, in the case of a sloped lot in the SC zone strict application of
the definition of building height would mean that the actual buildable area of the lot would be
substantially less on a sloped lot than a flat lot, which would deprive the property of the same
development potential compared to other properties within the same zone.

The requested variances are consistent with approved development of other properties with hotels
on sloped lots within the immediate vicinity of the project. The Hotel St. Lauren (231 Beacon
Street) and Casa Maraquita (229 Metropole Avenue) are hotel projects also developed in the SC
zone under the same development standards which exceed development standards, including
height, floor area, and lot coverage standards for the zone. According to the permitting records for
these projects, approval was granted because of the topography of the lots, and with
acknowledgement that while the hotels were larger than permitted by the development standards
for the zone, they fit within the context of the existing development and topography in the
surrounding area.

Therefore, it is the opinion of staff that the proposed variances may be granted in conformance
with the findings of the municipal code, as there are special circumstances related to lot topography
that would otherwise deprive the property of the development potential of other flat lots within the
same zone, and the variances do not constitute granting of special privileges and similar variances
have previously been granted for the same use on similarly sloped lots within the same zone.

Issue 2: Employee Housing

AMC Section 9-11.104.d requires that any new commercial development shall provide rental
housing for at least 50% of the peak season employees. The applicant has estimated that four full-
time employees will be employed by the business with the completion of both phases of the project.
The proposed project shall provide housing for four employees, consisting of one manager suite
and three housekeeper studio units on-site, which exceeds the housing requirements of the
municipal code.

There is no standard unit size requirement for employee housing units. However, all rentals must
be for the period of not less than six months to provide for housing stability for employees. Rents
for such accommodations may be established by the hotel operator with City approval.

The proposed project is subject to audit by the City following the first peak season after
commercial operations have commenced to ensure that a sufficient amount of employee housing
has been provided to accommodate at least 50% of peak season employees. The City reserves the
right to modify the new commercial development's rental space requirements in line with
municipal code requirements if the estimation in this application is deficient.

  7
65059.00002\42583158.2
 Issue 3: Parking

The applicant proposes to provide on-site autoette parking space for the project. This space is to
be designated for parking of a commercial autoette to service the hotel. The vehicle will be parked
in a covered parking space at the southwest corner of the building, with access to Metropole
Avenue. An existing striped loading zone on Metropole Avenue will be maintained to facilitate
commercial deliveries, and a new 3-minute loading zone is proposed to be added at the entrance
of the hotel on Beacon Street, as shown on the site plan in Attachment 3. The Beacon Street
loading zone may also serve as a designated stop for the Avalon COAST transit system.

The four employee housing units may qualify for residential autoette permits, subject to the
municipal code residency requirements for residential autoette permits. Resident employees will
not have access to the parking space reserved for the commercial autoette.

Per AMC Section 9-6.304, the number off-street parking spaces required for a development may
be determined by the Planning Commission as part of the review of the project application. The
Planning Commission may consider factors such as operational characteristics, site layout, and
surrounding development when considering approval of off-street parking.

It is the opinion of staff that the proposed parking plan can be found sufficient for the proposed
hotel operation. The primary use of the property will be transitory housing and guests are
anticipated to be dropped off by a rideshare (such as a taxi or other transport vehicle) at the curb
at Beacon Street where they would enter the hotel lobby. This will prevent interference with
circulation at the corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street, which is a heavily used
intersection. Designated parking for the commercial autoette, combined with the adjacent loading
zone, will ensure that commercial vehicles do not block traffic along Metropole Avenue, which is
functionally narrow due to on-street parking on both sides of the street.

It is possible that up to four additional autoettes could be parked on the street, if resident employees
meet the 9+ month residency requirement for a residential autoette permit, which is not guaranteed.
However, this is a small number of vehicles compared to the overall number of autoettes permitted
within the city and is not anticipated to have a substantial impact on the available on-street parking
within the “Flats” and surrounding areas.

Issue 4: Rooftop Deck Operations

According to the applicant, the rooftop deck will be a gathering place for hotel guests to sit and
enjoy the views of Avalon Bay and the surrounding hillsides. The rooftop deck is designed with a
600 SF building that is a combination prep kitchen/bar/restroom where hotel guests can purchase
beverages (including alcohol) and light food, such as tapas, salads and appetizers. The rooftop
deck food and beverage service will also be open to the public. The rooftop deck will be open from
7:00 AM until 10:00 PM. Weddings and other events may be held on the rooftop deck, however,
each event will be required to apply for a Special Event Permit (AMC Chapter 4-6) and
demonstrate compliance with all city code requirements.

  8
65059.00002\42583158.2
 Use of the rooftop deck has the potential to create noise nuisance for surrounding properties.
Operations must be consistent with Avalon Municipal Code Section 5-13.08 for a building within
Noise District 3, which states that it is “unlawful to use or operate or cause to be used or operated
outdoors any radio receiving set, sound amplifying equipment, television set, or other machine or
device which produces or reproduces sound in such a manner as to be plainly audible from the real
property line on which the sound amplifying equipment is located unless permitted by Special Use
Permit.” The applicant is not requesting approval of a Special Use Permit at this time.

It is the opinion of staff that with limited hours of operation and the requirement for a Special
Event Permit for events, the proposed roof deck is compatible with the intent of the SC zone and
should not cause undue noise nuisance to surrounding properties. The roof deck is surrounded by
a glass railing along the parapet wall, and the rooftop kitchen and mechanical equipment building
is placed to provide separation between the deck and adjacent residential uses to the east and south.
This conclusion is further supported by the Noise Impact Analysis prepared for the project,
provided as Appendix B of Attachment 6 of this report. The analysis concluded that with the roof
at maximum capacity (estimated 100 people), and with rooftop mechanical equipment operating,
the proposed project will increase noise levels by no more than 2 decibels over existing ambient
noise levels, which will not be a perceptible increase in general loudness to the human ear.

  GENERAL PLAN, LAND USE, AND ZONING COMPLIANCE

Annual Growth Policy:

The growth policy provides that new commercial development would only be permitted with
confirmation from Southern California Edison Company (“SCE”) that adequate fresh water is
available. The project involves permitting of a commercial business which requires an allocation
for water service. On June 7, 2024, SCE confirmed the availability of a water allocation for Phase
1 of the project (up to ten bedrooms). The allocation letter is included as Attachment 5. The
applicant has been placed on the waitlist for Phase II of the project. Staff has conditioned the
project in Condition 20 to require confirmation of a water allocation for Phase 2 prior to issuance
of any permits for improvements in that phase of site development. Staff recommends that, with
this Condition 20, the Planning Commission make the finding that the proposed project is in
compliance with the 2024 Annual Growth Policy.

Conditional Use Permit:

AMC Chapter 9-8.404 sets forth the required findings for approval of a Conditional Use Permit as
follows:

  1. The proposed conditional use shall conform with and carry out the certified Land Use
  Plan for the area. (AMC Section 9-8.404.a.1)

  The proposed project implements the following General Plan Goals and Policies:

  Policy II-9 of the Land Use Element:

  9
65059.00002\42583158.2
   “Encourage infill of the City Center area and where appropriate, increase the intensity of
  development on vacant and underutilized properties, in lieu of expanded development
  outward into Avalon’s hillsides, natural areas and open space.”

  The project proposed to demolish a vacant three-story apartment building and replace it
  with a new hotel with employee housing. The existing building has been vacant for over
  25 years and is in a state of disrepair. The project is designed to maximize the density of
  development on the property in the urbanized center of Avalon. Redevelopment of the
  project site will be an otherwise underutilized property back into productive use within the
  community and does not contribute to outward expansion into the surrounding natural areas
  or open spaces at the perimeter of the city.

  Policy II-12 of the Land Use Element:

  “Require infill development to incorporate design elements with buffers and transitions in
  density, scale, and mass to assure compatibility with adjacent uses.”

  The proposed project is designed to fit within the density, scale, and mass of existing
  development at the intersection of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street. The topography
  of this area represents a transition point between the “Flats” and the increasingly steep
  hillsides to the south and west. Existing development, including the St. Lauren Hotel and
  multi-family residential uses to the south and west, reflect a precent for taking advantage
  of the sloping hillside to allow for denser, taller buildings that do not appear out of place
  within the context of the surrounding area.

  Policy II-20 and II-21 of the Land Use Element:

  “Pursue new developments and businesses that add to the City’s economic base,
  particularly those that general sales tax and transient occupancy tax.” “Expand lodging
  choices by attracting and retaining desirable and high-quality facilities to the community.”
  The proposed consists of a hotel which provides individual hotel rooms, employee housing,
  and on-site food service. The addition of more transient accommodations will provide an
  additional high-quality hotel option for visitors to the community and generate additional
  transient occupancy taxes.

  2. The nature, condition, and development of adjacent uses, buildings and structures
  shall be considered and no proposed conditional use shall be permitted where such
  use will adversely affect or be materially detrimental to said adjacent uses, buildings
  and structures. (AMC Section 9-8.404.a.2)

  The proposed project is consistent with adjacent land uses and building types. The sloped
  topography of the lot is unusual compared to the majority of other properties within the SC
  zone. This means that while the applicant is requesting a variances for height, lot area, and
  lot coverage, the overall mass and scale of the building has been designed to fit within the
  context of surrounding commercial and multi-family residential development. Though not
  required by the municipal code, the accessory restaurant/mechanical building on the

  10
65059.00002\42583158.2
   rooftop is intentionally placed to minimize potential impacts to the view of adjacent
  buildings to the harbor. Operations of the hotel, including roof deck, must comply with
  Avalon Municipal Code Section 5-13.08 for a building within Noise District 3. Sound must
  be contained to the boundaries of the property and no events will be permitted without
  granting of a Special Event Permit by the City Manager. Therefore, the proposed project
  will not adversely affect or be materially detrimental to said adjacent uses, buildings and
  structures.

  3. The site for a proposed conditional use shall be adequate in size and shape to
  accommodate the yards, walls, fences, parking and loading facilities, landscaping and
  other development features prescribed in this chapter or as required as a condition
  in order to integrate said use with the uses in the neighborhood. (AMC Section 9-
  8.404.a.3)

  With the requested variances for lot coverage, floor area, building height, and hotel room
  size, the proposed project complies with all development standards as set forth in AMC for
  development on the project site in the Special Commercial (SC) zone. Designated parking
  for a commercial autoette, combined with the adjacent loading and drop off zones, will
  ensure that traffic associate with operation of the business will not interfere with circulation
  at the corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street, which is a heavily used intersection.
  The project site is located in an area with access to all necessary utilities and services to
  support the proposed use, including electric, water, gas, sewer, saltwater, and internet.

  4. The site for a proposed conditional use shall be served by highways and streets
  adequate in width and improved as necessary to carry the kind and quantity of traffic
  such use would generate. (AMC Section 9-8.404.a.4)

  The project site is located at the southeast corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street.
  This is a heavily traveled intersection and both streets are identified as Major Circulation
  Facility in the General Plan Circulation Element. The primary use of the property will be
  transitory housing and guests are anticipated to be dropped off by a rideshare (such as a
  taxi or other transport vehicle) at the curb at Beacon Street where they would enter the
  hotel lobby. Designated parking for a commercial autoette, combined with the adjacent
  loading and drop off zones, will ensure that traffic associate with operation of the business
  will not interfere with circulation at the corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street,
  which is a heavily used intersection.

  5. The proposed conditional use shall be consistent with and carry out the purpose and
  intent of the underlying zone. (AMC Section 9-8.404.a.5)

  Per AMC Section 9-6.301, the SC zoning district is established as an area where both small
  scale residents and neighborhood retail and services can coexist harmoniously. Hotels and
  residential uses are permitted in the SC with approval of a Conditional Use Permit.

  The project proposes to develop a new hotel with individual hotel rooms, employee
  housing, and rooftop food service. This will provide a new transient accommodation option
  for visitors to the city as well as housing for local workers. This is consistent with the

  11
65059.00002\42583158.2
   underlying intent of the zone and compatible with surrounding development in the vicinity
  of the project site.

Variance:

AMC Chapter 9-8.405 sets forth the required findings for approval of a Variance as follows:

  1. Variances from the terms of the Zoning Ordinance shall be granted only when,
  because of special circumstances applicable to the property including size, shape,
  topography, location or surroundings, the strict application of the Zoning Ordinance
  deprives such property of privileges enjoyed by other property in the vicinity and
  under identical zoning classification.

  The urban fabric of Avalon is relatively compact, with approximately 80-90 acres of
  existing development already located within the valley floor and the immediately
  surrounding hillsides. Individually owned lots in Avalon comprise less than 1% of the total
  city acreage. Therefore, it is important to maximize the use of land within the city within
  the development parameters of each zoning district, so long as it is consistent with overall
  community character.

  ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINATION

California Environmental Quality Act:

The proposed project is categorically exempt from the provisions of the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15332 (Class 32 – In-fill Development Projects)
because it has no potential to have a significant effect on the environment.

The Class 32 reflects a determination by the California Office of Planning and Research (OPR)
that projects that meet the Class 32 criteria will not have a significant environmental effect and,
therefore, are exempt from CEQA. (Berkeley Hillside Preservation v. City of Berkeley (2015) 60
Cal.4th 1086, 1102.) To apply, a project must be an in-fill development and meet the following
criteria: (1) is consistent with the applicable General Plan designation and applicable policies, as
well as applicable zoning designations and regulations, (2) would occur on a site less than five (5)
acres, (3) the project site must have no habitat value, (4) the project would not result in significant
traffic, noise, air quality, or water quality effects, and (5) the site can be adequately served by all
required utilities and public services. The Class 32 exemption reflects the understanding that “the
majority of private projects for which a government permit or similar entitlement is necessary are

  17
65059.00002\42583158.2
 minor in scope … and hence, in the absence of unusual circumstances, have little or no effect on
the public environment.” (Pacific Palisades Residents Association, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles
(2023) 88 Cal.App.5th 1338, 1363.) If a project meets the criteria and qualifies for the Class 32
exemption, the project is categorically exempt from CEQA unless one of the exceptions to
exemptions apply. The exemption is not limited to any use type and may apply to residential,
commercial, industrial, public facility, and/or mixed-use projects.

The project meets all of the aforementioned requirements and is exempt under Class 32, as
supported by substantial evidence:

  a) General Plan and Zoning Consistency: The project site is designated Special Commercial

  The SC designation provides an area in which both small scale residents and neighborhood

  b) Less Than 5 Acres: The project site is approximately 3,225 square feet (0.07 acres), which

  c) No Habitat Value: The project site is located in an urban area currently developed with an
  three-story apartment building. Because of the existing site’s developed nature in a highly
  urban environment the site has no value as habitat for endangered, rare, or threatened
  species. There is no sensitive vegetation or habitat on-site. The project would not encroach

  d) No Significant Traffic, Noise, Air Quality or Water Quality Effects: Technical studies have

  in the City, particularly the residential zones, have additional detailed standards for
  measurement of building height (low slope, hillside, steep hillside) that account for the
  topography present within the zone to allow for equitable development of all lots. However,
  in the case of a sloped lot in the SC zone strict application of the definition of building
  height would mean that the actual buildable area of the lot would be substantially less on a
  sloped lot than a flat lot, which would deprive the property of the same development
  potential compared to other properties within the same zone.

  Therefore, the proposed variances may be granted in conformance with the findings of the
  municipal code, as there are special circumstances related to lot topography that would
  otherwise deprive the property of the development potential of other lots within the same
  zone that lack the sloped topography of this lot.

2. Any variance granted shall be subject to such conditions as will assure that the
  adjustment thereby authorized shall not constitute a grant of special privileges
  inconsistent with the limitations upon other properties in the vicinity and zone in
  which such property is situated.

  The requested variances are consistent with approved development of other properties with
  hotels on sloped lots within the immediate vicinity of the project in the SC zone. The Hotel
  St. Lauren (231 Beacon Street) and Casa Maraquita (229 Metropole Avenue) are hotel
  projects also developed in the SC zone under the same development standards which
  exceed development standards, including height, floor area, and lot coverage standards for
  the zone. According to the permitting records for these projects, approval was granted
  because of the topography of the lots, and with acknowledgement that while the hotels
  were larger than permitted by the development standards for the zone, they fit within the
  context of the existing development and topography in the surrounding area. Therefore,
  granting of the requested variances does not constitute granting of special privileges and
  similar variances have previously been granted for the same use on similarly sloped lots

  5
   within the same zone to allow for the equitable development of property within the SC
  zone.

  3. A variance shall not be granted for a parcel of property which authorizes a use or
  activity which is not otherwise expressly authorized by the zone regulation governing
  the parcel of property.

  Hotels and residential uses are conditionally permitted uses within the SC zone. The
  application does not include a request for any use that is not permitted within the zoning

  4. No variances shall be granted which reduce or adversely affect access to or along the

SECTION 2 – ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

The proposed project is categorically exempt from the provisions of the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15332 (Class 32 – In-fill Development Projects)
because it has no potential to have a significant effect on the environment.

The Class 32 reflects a determination by the California Office of Planning and Research (OPR)
that projects that meet the Class 32 criteria will not have a significant environmental effect and,
therefore, are exempt from CEQA. (Berkeley Hillside Preservation v. City of Berkeley (2015) 60
Cal.4th 1086, 1102.) To apply, a project must be an in-fill development and meet the following
criteria: (1) is consistent with the applicable General Plan designation and applicable policies, as
well as applicable zoning designations and regulations, (2) would occur on a site less than five (5)
acres, (3) the project site must have no habitat value, (4) the project would not result in significant
traffic, noise, air quality, or water quality effects, and (5) the site can be adequately served by all
required utilities and public services. The Class 32 exemption reflects the understanding that “the
majority of private projects for which a government permit or similar entitlement is necessary are
minor in scope … and hence, in the absence of unusual circumstances, have little or no effect on
the public environment.” (Pacific Palisades Residents Association, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles
(2023) 88 Cal.App.5th 1338, 1363.) If a project meets the criteria and qualifies for the Class 32
exemption, the project is categorically exempt from CEQA unless one of the exceptions to
exemptions apply. The exemption is not limited to any use type and may apply to residential,
commercial, industrial, public facility, and/or mixed-use projects.

The project meets all of the aforementioned requirements and is exempt under Class 32, as
supported by substantial evidence:

  a) General Plan and Zoning Consistency: The project site is designated Special Commercial
  (SC) by the General Plan Land Use Element and is located within the SC Zoning District.
  The SC designation provides an area in which both small scale residents and neighborhood
  retail and services can coexist harmoniously. Hotels and residential uses are permitted in
  the SC with approval of a Conditional Use Permit.
  b) Less Than 5 Acres: The project site is approximately 3,225 square feet (0.07 acres), which
  is less than five acres.
  c) No Habitat Value: The project site is located in an urban area currently developed with an
  three-story apartment building. Because of the existing site’s developed nature in a highly
  urban environment the site has no value as habitat for endangered, rare, or threatened
  species. There is no sensitive vegetation or habitat on-site. The project would not encroach

  10
   into any jurisdictional waters or areas that support native and/or sensitive habitat. The
  property does not contain any wetland areas.
  d) No Significant Traffic, Noise, Air Quality or Water Quality Effects: Technical studies have
  been prepared that analyze the potential impacts of the proposed project on the surrounding
  community related to traffic, noise, and air quality. These studies conclude that the project
  will not generate a significant number of new vehicle trips, increase the ambient noise
  levels by more than 2 decibels, or generate construction or operations related emissions
  beyond the thresholds adopted by the South Coast Air Quality Management District. The
  site is currently fully developed, and a non-priority Water Quality Management Plan will
  be required to be prepared at the time of grading permit review.
  e) Utilities and Public Services: All required utilities, including sewer, water, energy, are
  existing within the project site. Southern California Edison has issued a water allocation
  for Phase 1 of the project, for up to 10 bedrooms/units. All public services, including police
  and fire protection, are adequate to accommodate the project. As conditioned and designed,
  the project will be adequately served by all required utilities and public services

Furthermore, the project was evaluated pursuant to the criteria for the exceptions to the exemptions
as identified in Guidelines Section 14 CCR, Chapter 3, Article 19, Section 15300.2 and found that
there are no exceptions to the use of an exemption for the project. The Property does not impact
an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern, does not result in cumulative impacts,
does not have a significant effect on the environment due to unusual circumstances, does not
damage scenic resources within a state scenic highway, is not a hazardous waste site, and is not
identified as a historical resource. Therefore, no further analysis is required. A Notice of
Exemption will be filed with the County of Los Angeles Clerk of the Board.

 The Cameron Hotel

Project Description

The proposed Cameron Hotel is located on the south-west
corner of Beacon Street and Metropole in the City of Avalon. The
existing structure was originally built in 1923. With the intention
of providing housing for the Cameron family whom occupied the
building for over 30 years. However the existing building has
been vacant for the last 30 years and has fallen into a serious
state of disrepair. Numerous unsuccessful options have been
proposed to the Cameron family relating to bringing this building
back to life. The Cameron family has entered to an agreement
with Hamilton Pacific which will allow the revival of this site.

Rehabilitation of the existing structure was considered and it was
determined to be infeasible because of the integrity of the
existing structure. Plumbing, electrical, HVAC, fires sprinklers do
not meet any of todays building codes and requirements. Severe
termite infestation and sub standard structural issues are
prevalent in the existing structure. Therefore it has been
determined to remove the existing building with a new structure
that can provide to the community uses that are desperately
needed.

Currently, Avalon is desperately in need employee housing for
both year round housing as well as daily workforce housing. This
type of housing is a strong component of the new proposed plan.

  2  PROJECT OVERVIEW

2.1  Introduction

Pursuant to Section 15367 of the State CEQA Guidelines, the City of Avalon (City) is the public agency that
has the principal responsibility for conducting or approving a project.

Applicant Hamilton Pacific, LLC, Inc proposes to demolish the existing vacant building on APN 7480-031-
040, which is a 3,325 SF lot on the southeast corner of Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue and construct
a hotel. The Proposed Project would demolish the existing, vacant, 5,882 square foot (SF) three-story
residential building that is up to 44 feet high (northeast building corner) and contains 10 units and
construct a new 12,212 SF four-story hotel at a maximum height of 28 feet at the parapet (southwest
building corner), that would include 37 hotel rooms, four hotel employee studio units and a rooftop deck
that includes accessory structures of an elevator and combination outdoor prep kitchen/bathroom
structure that would provide light food and beverage service where the accessory structures would
extend approximately 10 feet above the parapet.

Demolition of the existing building would occur with labor and hand power tools, and no heavy equipment
would be utilized except to prepare the building pad for final grading once the building demolition has
been completed. Interior room completion would be completed in two phases, based on water allocations
by Southern California Edison which dictates development in the City based its operation of the City’s
water system. Operations consist of that for a typical hotel. The Project Site is zoned as Special Commercial
(SC).

The City, as the lead agency for the Proposed Project, is responsible for preparing environmental
documentation in accordance with CEQA to determine if approval of the discretionary actions requested
and subsequent development of the Proposed Project would have a significant impact on the
environment. As such, this document is designed to meet the requirements for the City of Avalon’s
Environmental Assessment/CEQA compliance.

2.2  Background

Applicant Hamilton Pacific, LLC offers full service general contracting services throughout Southern
California. The Applicant is also currently the developer and contractor for the Hamilton Cove
Development in Avalon, and currently has approximately 15 to 30 construction employees working on
any given day depending on the work activity. The Applicant currently houses employees during the week
in a combination of hotels and other transient housing. Given the housing shortage in the City of Avalon
and the Hamilton Cove development is anticipated to continue for another five to 10 years, the Applicant
has chosen to lease and redevelop the existing building at 301 Beacon Street for the purpose of providing
a more permanent solution to the long-term temporary housing needs of its Hamilton Cove construction
employees and develop/operate a hotel to off-set the costs of the building development. It is anticipated
that housing his employees in this development would free up approximately 10 to 20 rooms in hotels
and in other transient housing in Avalon.

The building at 301 Beacon Street has been vacant for more than 20 years, is in a state of disrepair, and
has become somewhat of an eyesore in a prominent area of the City. A structural evaluation of the
building conducted by the applicant has determined that remodeling or renovating the building is not
feasible, and it must be completely demolished and reconstructed.

Therefore, the Applicant is proposing to demolish the building and reconstruct it to current standards. All
of the 37 hotel rooms range from 200 to 230 SF, which is greater than the 190 SF as required by Avalon
Municipal Code Section 9-7.901, and the bathrooms average 50 SF, which is greater than the 35 SF
required by the City code. An additional four studio apartments are provided for the hotel manager and
housekeeping staff.

Once completed, the Applicant would contract with the hotel operator for exclusive rights to use three to
four hotel rooms during the weekdays for the Hamilton Cove construction workers, who are currently
housed in various transient housing and hotels throughout the City. These rooms would be released for
visitors and/or other workforce housing on the weekends.

The Applicant has identified that the benefits of this Project to the City include the following:

  •  Additional transient occupancy taxes for 37 hotel rooms;

  •  Additional availability of hotel rooms for visitors;

  •  Create four to five new jobs for administration and other duties, with four jobs offering live-in
  accommodations as hotel workforce housing.

The proposed Project is located at the southeast corner of Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue in the
City of Avalon and is identified as 301 Beacon Street, Los Angeles County Assessor Parcel No. (APN) 7480-
031-040. Refer to Figure 1: Regional Vicinity and Figure 2: Project Location located at the end of this

2.3.1  Existing Conditions

The building and Proposed Project is situated on the southeast corner of Metropole Avenue and Beacon
Street.

The Project Site is vacant 5,882 SF three-story, 22-foot-high building that contains 10 residential units. The
existing building footprint occupies approximately 2,859 SF of the 3,325 SF lot, with an approximately 466
SF patio, which represents an approximately 19-foot-wide setback.

The three-story building was constructed in 1923, designed in a vernacular style with elements of
Mediterranean Revival. The building includes two shallow wings that project from the east and south
corners. The building has a flat roof that has a centralized stepped parapet at the northwest elevation.
The stepped parapet meets in the center of the northwest elevation and includes a tower-like projection
with a hipped roof that is approximately 34 feet tall. The main roof is rolled asphalt, and the tower
projection structure is clad with shingles. The building is wood frame construction, sheathed in non-
original vinyl siding.

It was constructed with some units existing below the street grade, which allows the roofline to remain
flat, similar to the neighboring buildings along Metropole Avenue which also have units below street grade
due to the street’s steep slope. Therefore, the above-ground elevation of the building is shorter along the
rear of the building at Metropole Avenue than it is along the frontage at Metropole Avenue and Beacon
Street. The existing building height is 22 feet at the rear of the property.

There are recessed ground-level entrances at all four elevations, framed by archways and accessed by
concrete steps with original wood landings. All doors except one are wooden with multi-pane glazing. The
northeast elevation contains recessed entrances framed by archways that lead to a metal fire escape on
the upper levels. The entrance on the southwest elevation is surrounded by a metal canopy. Fenestration
appears to be original consisting of double-hung, one over wood frame windows with lambs tongue
details. The first-floor windows on all elevations are covered with wooden lattices.

There is one Pepper tree at the rear of the building. There is no other vegetation, or habitat for sensitive
species.

The existing building housed short-term and seasonal visitors after its construction in 1923 and was also
occupied by the property owner’s family between approximately 1930 and 2000. However, it has been
vacant since approximately 2000 and has fallen into a state of disrepair. The building does not meet
current building code standards and significant termite damage is present.

2.4  Project Description

Applicant Hamilton Pacific, LLC, Inc proposes to demolish the existing vacant building on APN 7480-031-
040, which is a 3,325 SF lot on the southeast corner of Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue (a cross-
sloped lot) and construct a hotel. The Proposed Project would demolish the existing, vacant, 5,882 square
foot (SF) three-story residential building that is 22 feet high (southwest building corner) and contains 10
units and construct a new 12,212 SF four-story hotel at a maximum height of 44 feet at the parapet
(northeast building corner), that would include 37 hotel rooms, four hotel employee studio units and a
rooftop deck with an elevator (80 SF) and a bathroom and outdoor prep kitchen accessory structures
(total 480 SF) that would extend approximately 10 feet above the parapet.

The existing building has been determined to be in an extremely deteriorated state, structurally deficient,
and demolition is required. Demolition of the existing building would occur with labor and hand power
tools only, and no heavy equipment would be utilized except to prepare the building pad for final grading
once the building demolition has been completed.

Operations consist of use of typical hotel operations. Once completed, the Applicant would contract with
the hotel management for exclusive rights to use three to four hotel rooms during the week for his
Hamilton Cove construction crew, and these rooms would be available to visitors and other workforce
housing on the weekends.

The Proposed Project would generally occupy the same building footprint as the existing building but

2.4.2  Construction Characteristics

Initial site improvements include demolition, grading and underground infrastructure followed by building
construction and painting activities. Site grading would be limited to minor removal and soil balancing
with little to no import or export of fill material. Project construction would require the use of heavy
equipment such as one backhoe, concrete trucks, and a water truck.

It is anticipated that the entire property boundary would be fenced and screened.

All construction would occur in accordance with City guidelines, Section 5-13.06, which makes
construction within 500 feet of residential zones, hotels, or motels unlawful between the hours of 7:00
p.m. and 8:00 a.m. or at any time on Sundays.

Construction Phasing

The Project would be developed in two phases based on the SCE water allotments for the property. In
accordance with SCE water allotment guidelines, the Project can currently only occupy rooms that make
up a total of 10 water units until SCE develops additional capital improvements, the schedule of which is
unknown at this time, but is anticipated to be near the end of 2025. With these capital improvements in
place, SCE would be able to serve water to the additional 34 units, or a total of 44 water units for the hotel
rooms. Additional water credits from SCE to operate the roof-top restaurant would be required prior to
operation.

The following construction phasing is anticipated, although may change, based on the water credits issued
by SCE.

Phase 1 is anticipated to occur between September 2024 and January 2026 (10 total water units), but may
vary depending on construction crew scheduling:

  •  Demolition, final grading, utilities as needed.
  •  Build the hotel infrastructure, exterior/architectural, install elevator to all four floors with rooftop
  access, all mechanical to fully support first phase.
  •  Develop first floor interior that would contain lobby, seven private, double-occupancy hotel rooms,
  and one manager’s apartment, (8 water units). All hotel rooms in this phase would be designed for
  two persons per room, in accordance with SCE water allotment standards.
  •  Develop second floor interior with 1 of the 10 planned hotel rooms and 1 housekeeper suite (2
  water units).
  •  Develop third and fourth floors to rough-in only with fire sprinklers.

It is the intent that the facilities and rooms developed during Phase 1 would be occupied upon completion
of Phase 1.

2.4.3  Operational Characteristics

General Hotel

The Project would operate as a typical 37-room hotel that would be staffed 24 hours per day, seven days
per week by staff that live on site at the hotel. The Applicant intends, upon occupancy, to enter into an
exclusive contract with the hotel operator for use of at least three hotel rooms for the Applicant’s
construction crews Monday nights through Thursday nights, leaving the open to rent out to visitors and
other workforce housing Friday nights through Sunday nights.

Visitors are anticipated to arrive on foot or by one of the many transit services available in the city, similar
to other hotel operations in the city. Passenger off-loading would occur along the hotel’s entrance (Beacon
Street).

The Proposed Project is anticipated to generate four to five new jobs for hotel reception/administration,
one hotel live-in manager, and three live-in housekeepers.

Rooftop Deck

The rooftop deck would be a gathering place for hotel guests to sit and enjoy the view. The 2,580 SF
rooftop deck would be accessed by an elevator (80 SF) and is designed with approximately 1,800 SF of
outdoor seating, and a 480 SF structure that is a combination prep kitchen/bar/restrooms where guests
can purchase beverages (including alcohol) and light food, such as tapas, salads and appetizers. The
rooftop deck food and beverage service would be for hotel guests and the general public.

construction specifications to avoid potential impacts to environmental resources. The City would also
include the applicant-proposed measures as Conditions of Approval. These include but are not limited to

  annoyance to any considerable number of persons or to the public, or which endanger the
  comfort, repose, health or safety of any such persons or the public, or which cause, or have a
  natural tendency to cause, injury or damage to business or property.

  o  SCAQMD Rule 403: Governs emissions of fugitive dust during construction and operation
  activities. Compliance with this rule is achieved through application of standard Best
  Management Practices, such as application of water or chemical stabilizers to disturbed soils,
  covering haul vehicles, restricting vehicle speeds on unpaved roads to 15 miles per hour,
  sweeping loose dirt from paved site access roadways, cessation of construction activity when

  3  REGULATORY SUMMARY

The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) is codified in Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations
(14 CCR). This statute requires state and local agencies to identify the significant environmental impacts
of their actions and to avoid or mitigate those impacts, if feasible. Guidelines for implementation of the
statute are the regulations that explain and interpret the law for both the public agencies required to
administer CEQA and for the public. They are found in the California Code of Regulations, in Chapter 3 of
Title 14 “Guidelines for Implementation of the California Environmental Quality Act” (Guidelines).

Definition of a Project. Guidelines Section 15378 defines a Project as “the whole of an action, which has
a potential for resulting in either a direct physical change in the environment, or a reasonably foreseeable
indirect physical change in the environment, and that is any of the following:

  (1) An activity directly undertaken by any public agency including but not limited to public works construction
  and related activities clearing or grading of land, improvements to existing public structures, enactment and
  amendment of zoning ordinances, and the adoption and amendment of local General Plans or elements thereof
  pursuant to Government Code Sections 65100-65700.

  (2) An activity undertaken by a person which is supported in whole or in part through public agency contracts,
  grants, subsidies, loans, or other forms of assistance from one or more public agencies.

  (3) An activity involving the issuance to a person of a lease, permit, license, certificate, or other entitlement for
  use by one or more public agencies.

The proposed action is to approve the Project identified as Proposed Cameron Hotel at 301 Beacon
Street, an application by Hamilton Pacific, LLC for the demolition of an existing multi-story residential
building and construction of a 37-room hotel, which qualifies as a Project under the CEQA Guidelines
because the Projects the Project must be approved by a discretionary action by the City of Avalon,
Planning Commission Application No. 2842.

Exemption Review. CEQA Section 15061 (a) states that once a lead agency determines that the activity
is a project under CEQA, the lead agency shall determine if the Project is exempt from CEQA. A Project is
exempt from CEQA if the following apply (Section 15061[b]):

  1) The project is exempt by statute (see, e.g. Article 18, commencing with Section 15260).

  2) The project is exempt pursuant to a categorical exemption (see Article 19, commencing with Section
  15300) and the application of that categorical exemption is not barred by one of the exceptions set
  forth in Section 15300.2.

  3) The activity is covered by the common sense exemption that CEQA applies only to projects which have
  the potential for causing a significant effect on the environment. Where it can be seen with certainty
  that there is no possibility that the activity in question may have a significant effect on the environment,
  the activity is not subject to CEQA.

  4) The project will be rejected or disapproved by a public agency. (See Section 15270(b)).

  5) The project is exempt pursuant to the provisions of Article 12.5 of this Chapter.

would be barred under the exemption class. These exceptions include 1:

  (a) Location. Classes 3, 4, 5, 6, and 11 are qualified by consideration of where the project is to be located -- a

  environment be significant. Therefore, these classes are considered to apply all instances, except where the
  project may impact on an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern where designated, precisely
  mapped, and officially adopted pursuant to law by federal, state, or local agencies.

  (b) Cumulative Impact. All exemptions for these classes are inapplicable when the cumulative impact of

  (c) Significant Effect. A categorical exemption shall not be used for an activity where there is a reasonable
  possibility that the activity will have a significant effect on the environment due to unusual circumstances.

  (d) Scenic Highways. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project which may result in damage to

  within a highway officially designated as a state scenic highway. This does not apply to improvements which

  (e) Hazardous Waste Sites. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project located on a site which is

  Trip Reduction Calculation Due to Transportation Mode

  Due to the growing number of urban in-fill projects where other modes of transportation could be
  used, the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) in 2009, commissioned a study of travel
  characteristics of in-fill development in California’s metropolitan areas (Study). 2 The Study noted that
  during local land use review and development permitting processes, public agencies commonly
  require estimates of vehicle travel impacts associated with proposed land use projects, assessments
  of their potential contribution to traffic congestion, and identification of appropriate mitigation
  strategies. These strategies often include mitigation fees, private developer contributions, special tax
  assessment districts, and specific infrastructure improvements.

  In preparing traffic and transportation impact analyses, professionals often rely on the ITE published
  trip-generation rates for various types of land uses. However, ITE data typically reflects isolated
  suburban development usually lacking availability and proximity of transit service, and the ITE study
  sites are located such that they are difficult to access by walking or bicycling. The Study indicated that
  the use of ITE trip-generation rates for proposed urban in-fill development projects served by transit
  and having good pedestrian access could significantly over- predict vehicular traffic impacts. The Study
  evaluated various land uses, such as high-rise apartments, retail, office, and several restaurant types.

  A hotel/motel was not among the land uses studied. However, the result of the Study was that for all
  land uses studied, the ITE calculation rate was an average of 35 percent higher in the AM and 26
  percent higher in the PM than what was actually observed.

  Study Methodology

  Three 15-minute ambient noise measurements were conducted at the project site on May 1, 2024.

  noise measurements were taken to determine the existing ambient noise levels. Noise data indicates

  The Project’s potential noise was modeled using SoundPLAN (SP) acoustical modeling software that is
  capable of evaluating multiple stationary noise source impacts at various receiver locations. SP’s
  software utilizes algorithms (based on the inverse square law and reference equipment noise level
  data) to calculate noise level projections. The software allows the user to input specific noise sources,
  spectral content, sound barriers, building placement, topography, and sensitive receptor locations.

(a) Location. Classes 3, 4, 5, 6, and 11 are qualified by consideration of where the project is to be located -

environment be significant. Therefore, these classes are considered to apply all instances, except where
the project may impact on an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern where designated,
precisely mapped, and officially adopted pursuant to law by federal, state, or local agencies.

  Discussion. The Project qualifies as Class 32. Therefore, this exception criterion is not applicable.

(b) Cumulative Impact. All exemptions for these classes are inapplicable when the cumulative impact of
successive projects of the same type in the same place, over time is significant.

(c) Significant Effect. A categorical exemption shall not be used for an activity where there is a reasonable

2.1  Human Response to Changes in Noise Levels
In general, the healthy human ear is most sensitive to sounds between 1,000 Hz and 5,000 Hz (A-
weighted scale), and it perceives a sound within that range as being more intense than a sound with a
higher or lower frequency with the same magnitude. For purposes of this report, as well as with most
environmental documents, the A-scale weighting is typically reported in terms of A-weighted decibel
(dBA). Typically, the human ear can barely perceive the change in noise level of 3 dB. A change in 5 dB is
readily perceptible, and a change in 10 dB is perceived as being twice or half as loud. As previously
discussed, a doubling of sound energy results in a 3 dB increase in sound, which means that a doubling
of sound energy (e.g., doubling the volume of traffic on a highway) would result in a barely perceptible
change in sound level.

2.2  Noise Descriptors
Noise in our daily environment fluctuates over time. Some noise levels occur in regular patterns, others
are random. Some noise levels are constant, while others are sporadic. Noise descriptors were created
to describe the different time-varying noise levels.

A-Weighted Sound Level: The sound pressure level in decibels as measured on a sound level meter using
the A-weighted filter network. The A-weighting filter de-emphasizes the very low and very high-frequency
components of the sound in a manner similar to the response of the human ear. A numerical method of
rating human judgment of loudness.

Ambient Noise Level: The composite of noise from all sources, near and far. In this context, the ambient
noise level constitutes the normal or existing level of environmental noise at a given location.

Community Noise Equivalent Level (CNEL): The average equivalent A-weighted sound level during a 24-
hour day, obtained after the addition of five (5) decibels to sound levels in the evening from 7:00 to 10:00
PM and after the addition of ten (10) decibels to sound levels in the night before 7:00 AM and after 10:00
PM.

Decibel (dB): A unit for measuring the amplitude of a sound equal to 20 times the logarithm to the base
10 of the ratio of the pressure of the sound measured to the reference pressure, which is 20 micro-pascals.

dB(A): A-weighted sound level (see definition above).

noise level during the sample period.

Habitable Room: Any room meeting the requirements of the Uniform Building Code or other applicable
regulations which is intended to be used for sleeping, living, cooking, or dining purposes, excluding such
enclosed spaces as closets, pantries, bath or toilet rooms, service rooms, connecting corridors, laundries,
unfinished attics, foyers, storage spaces, cellars, utility rooms, and similar spaces.

L(n): The A-weighted sound level exceeded during a certain percentage of the sample time. For example,
L10 in the sound level exceeded 10 percent of the sample time. Similarly L50, L90 and L99, etc.

Noise: Any unwanted sound or sound that is undesirable because it interferes with speech and hearing, is
intense enough to damage hearing, or is otherwise annoying. The State Noise Control Act defines noise as
"...excessive undesirable sound...".

Outdoor Living Area: Outdoor spaces that are associated with residential land uses typically used for
passive recreational activities or other noise-sensitive uses. Such spaces include patio areas, barbecue
areas, jacuzzi areas, etc., associated with residential uses; outdoor patient recovery or resting areas
associated with hospitals, convalescent hospitals, or rest homes; outdoor areas associated with places of
worship which have a significant role in services or other noise-sensitive activities; and outdoor school
facilities routinely used for educational purposes which may be adversely impacted by noise. Outdoor
areas usually not included in this definition are: front yard areas, driveways, greenbelts, maintenance
areas, and storage areas associated with residential land uses; exterior areas at hospitals that are not used
for patient activities; outdoor areas associated with places of worship and principally used for short-term
social gatherings; and, outdoor areas associated with school facilities that are not typically associated with
educational uses prone to adverse noise impacts (for example, school play yard areas).

Percent Noise Levels: See L(n).

Sound Level (Noise Level): The weighted sound pressure level obtained by use of a sound level meter
having a standard frequency-filter for attenuating part of the sound spectrum.

4.2  SoundPLAN Acoustic Model
SoundPLAN (SP) acoustical modeling software was utilized to model future worst-case stationary noise
impacts to the adjacent land uses. SP is capable of evaluating multiple stationary noise source impacts at
various receiver locations. SP’s software utilizes algorithms (based on the inverse square law and reference
equipment noise level data) to calculate noise level projections. The software allows the user to input
specific noise sources, spectral content, sound barriers, building placement, topography, and sensitive
receptor locations.

The future worst-case noise level projections were modeled using referenced sound level data for the
various stationary on-site sources (rooftop mechanical equipment, crowd noise). The roof will include 16
rooftop AC units in a designated mechanical area and a maximum of 70 to 90 people for rooftop events. As
a worst-case scenario, the model assumes that the 16 rooftop AC units are operating simultaneously and
continuously in the mechanical area and that the maximum crowd capacity (approximately 90 people) is
gathered on the roof throughout the hour, and 50% of people talking at the same time. Each AC unit will
have a sound power level of 68 dBA. The 16 rooftop units were modeled as four (4) point sources. Each
point source represents four (4) AC units with a total sound power level of 74 dBA. The crowd of 90 people
was modeled as an area source within SoundPLAN. Appendix E provides the SoundPLAN inputs and outputs.

4.3  FHWA Traffic Noise Model
The traffic noise analysis utilizes the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Traffic Noise Model, together
with several key construction parameters. Key input speed, site conditions, trip generation, and vehicle mix
data. The modeling does not take into account any existing barriers, structures, and/or topographical
features that may further reduce noise levels.

Construction activities can produce vibration that may be felt by adjacent land uses. The construction of the

large bulldozer. A bulldozer has a vibration impact of 0.089 inches per second peak particle velocity (PPV)
at 25 feet which is likely perceptible but below any risk of architectural damage.

5.0  Traffic Noise Level Projections
Traffic noise along Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street will be the main source of noise impacting the
project site and the surrounding area. The Project projects 368 daily trips per CalEEMod. MD understands
that many of the vehicles in the City of Avalon are gas golf carts, which are often louder than typical
automobiles, as noted during the field visit. Thus, MD adjusted the vehicle distribution to 33% automobiles
and 67% medium trucks to account for the louder golf carts. The model assumes that one-third (92) of the
trips occur along Metropole Avenue and that two-thirds (276) occur along Beacon Street. Project-only traffic
noise levels are anticipated to be 51 dBA Leq along Metropole Avenue and 56 dBA Leq along Beacon Street
during daytime hours (see Appendix D). The project will thus increase the existing traffic noise level by a
maximum of 2 dB. It takes a change of 3 dB or more for the human ear to perceive a difference. Therefore,
the impact is less than significant.

7.3 are taken. See Appendix F for calculations.

7.3  Construction Noise and Vibration Reduction Best Management Practices
Construction operations must follow the City’s Noise Ordinance, which states that construction, repair,
or excavation work performed must occur within the permissible hours. To further ensure that
construction activities do not disrupt the adjacent land uses, the following best management practices
are recommended:

  1. Ensure construction occurs during the hours of 8AM to 7PM on weekdays and Saturdays and at
  no time on Sundays, in accordance with the City of Avalon’s Noise Ordinance.

  2. Equip all construction equipment with 15 dB mufflers.

  3. Locate equipment staging areas as far away as possible from the sensitive receptors.

  4. Utilize heavy equipment no less than 10’ away from existing buildings.

  5. Turn off idling equipment when not in use.

  6. Maintain equipment so that vehicles and their loads are secured from rattling and banging.

Glossary of Acoustical Terms
  Glossary of Terms

A-Weighted Sound Level: The sound pressure level in decibels as measured on a sound level meter
using the A-weighted filter network. The A-weighting filter de-emphasizes the very low and very
high-frequency components of the sound in a manner similar to the response of the human ear. A
numerical method of rating human judgment of loudness.

Ambient Noise Level: The composite of noise from all sources, near and far. In this context, the
ambient noise level constitutes the normal or existing level of environmental noise at a given
location.

Community Noise Equivalent Level (CNEL): The average equivalent A-weighted sound level during
a 24-hour day, obtained after the addition of five (5) decibels to sound levels in the evening from
7:00 to 10:00 PM and after the addition of ten (10) decibels to sound levels in the night before 7:00
AM and after 10:00 PM.

Decibel (dB): A unit for measuring the amplitude of a sound, equal to 20 times the logarithm to the
base 10 of the ratio of the pressure of the sound measured to the reference pressure, which is 20
micro-pascals.

dB(A): A-weighted sound level (see definition above).

Equivalent Sound Level (LEQ): The sound level corresponding to a steady noise level over a given
sample period with the same amount of acoustic energy as the actual time-varying noise level. The
energy average noise level during the sample period.

Habitable Room: Any room meeting the requirements of the Uniform Building Code or other
applicable regulations which is intended to be used for sleeping, living, cooking, or dining purposes,
excluding such enclosed spaces as closets, pantries, bath or toilet rooms, service rooms, connecting
corridors, laundries, unfinished attics, foyers, storage spaces, cellars, utility rooms, and similar
spaces.

L(n): The A-weighted sound level exceeded during a certain percentage of the sample time. For
example, L10 in the sound level exceeded 10 percent of the sample time. Similarly L50, L90, L99,
etc.

Noise: Any unwanted sound or sound which is undesirable because it interferes with speech and
hearing or is intense enough to damage hearing, or is otherwise annoying. The State Noise Control
Act defines noise as “...excessive undesirable sound...”.
 Noise Criteria (NC) Method: This metric plots octave band sound levels against a family of reference
curves, with the number rating equal to the highest tangent line value as demonstrated in Figure
1.
  FIGURE 1: Sample NC Curves and
Percent Noise Levels: See L(n).
  Sample Spectrum Levels
Room Criterion (RC) Method: When sound quality
in the space is important, the RC metric provides a
diagnostic tool to quantify both the speech
interference level and spectral imbalance.

Sound Level (Noise Level): The weighted sound
pressure level obtained by use of a sound level
meter having a standard frequency filter for
attenuating part of the sound spectrum.

Sound Level Meter: An instrument, including a
microphone, an amplifier, an output meter, and
frequency  weighting  networks  for  the
measurement and determination of noise and
sound levels.

Sound Transmission Class (STC): To quantify STC, a Transmission Loss (TL) measurement is
performed in a laboratory over a range of 16 third-octave bands between 125 – 4,000 Hertz (Hz).
The average human voice creates sound within the 125 – 4,000 Hz 1/3rd octave bands.

STC is a single-number rating given to a particular material or assembly. The STC rating measures
the ability of a material or an assembly to resist airborne sound transfer over the specified
frequencies (see ASTM International Classification E413 and E90). In general, a higher STC rating
corresponds with a greater reduction of noise transmitting through a partition.

STC is highly dependent on the construction of the partition. The STC of a partition can be increased
by: adding mass, increasing or adding air space, and adding absorptive materials within the
assembly. The STC rating does not assess low-frequency sound transfer (e.g. sounds less than 125
Hz). Special consideration must be given to spaces where the noise transfer concern has lower
frequencies than speech, such as mechanical equipment and or/or music. The STC rating is a lab test
that does not take into consideration weak points, penetrations, or flanking paths.

Even with a high STC rating, any penetration, air-gap, or “flanking path can seriously degrade the
isolation quality of a wall. Flanking paths are the means for sound to transfer from one space to
another other than through the wall. Sound can flank over, under, or around a wall. Sound can also
travel through common ductwork, plumbing, or corridors. Noise will travel between spaces at the
weakest points. Typically, there is no reason to spend money or effort to improve the walls until all
weak points are controlled first.
 Outdoor Living Area: Outdoor spaces that are associated with residential land uses typically used
for passive recreational activities or other noise-sensitive uses. Such spaces include patio areas,
barbecue areas, jacuzzi areas, etc. associated with residential uses; outdoor patient recovery or
resting areas associated with hospitals, convalescent hospitals, or rest homes; outdoor areas
associated with places of worship which have a significant role in services or other noise-sensitive
activities; and outdoor school facilities routinely used for educational purposes which may be
adversely impacted by noise. Outdoor areas usually not included in this definition are: front yard
areas, driveways, greenbelts, maintenance areas and storage areas associated with residential land
uses; exterior areas at hospitals that are not used for patient activities; outdoor areas associated
with places of worship and principally used for short-term social gatherings; and, outdoor areas
associated with school facilities that are not typically associated with educational uses prone to
adverse noise impacts (for example, school play yard areas).

Percent Noise Levels: See L(n).

Sound Level (Noise Level): The weighted sound pressure level obtained by use of a sound level
meter having a standard frequency filter for attenuating part of the sound spectrum.

Sound Level Meter: An instrument, including a microphone, an amplifier, an output meter, and
frequency weighting networks for the measurement and determination of noise and sound levels.

Single Event Noise Exposure Level (SENEL): The dB(A) level which, if it lasted for one second, would
produce the same A-weighted sound energy as the actual event.
