Subject:
301 Beacon Street Hotel – Focused Air Quality Impact Study, City of Avalon, CA

Dear Michael:
MD Acoustics, LLC (MD) has completed a focused Air Quality Impact Evaluation for the proposed
hotel project located at 301 Beacon Street in the City of Avalon, CA. The purpose of this focused
study is to evaluate the air quality construction and operational emissions generated by the proposed
project and to compare the project emissions to South Coast Air Quality Management District’s
(SCAQMD) thresholds of significance as it relates to residential and commercial uses and consistency
to the City’s General Plan. A list of definitions and terminology is located in Appendix A.
1.0  Project Description
The Project site is located at 301 Beacon Street within the City of Avalon, California, as shown in Exhibit
A. The site is currently zoned as Special Commercial. Land zoning surrounding the site includes
Special Commercial to the north, south, southeast, and west, and Commercial to the northeast.
Metropole Avenue is to the northwest, and Beacon Street is to the northeast. The Catalina
Airport is located approximately 6 miles northwest of the Project site.

The Project proposes a four (4) story hotel with multiple uses consisting of 35 hotel rooms, three (3)
onsite studio apartments (manager and two housekeepers), six (6) rooms with a separate
entrance for 6-12 workers, and a rooftop deck for guests. The hotel will also include a lobby, front
desk, and laundry/storage facilities. See Appendix B for the architectural plans.
2.0  Thresholds of Significance
Project emissions were compared to both regional and localized SCAQMD’s thresholds of significance
for construction and operational emissions1,2.

3.0  Evaluation Procedure/Methodology
MD utilized the latest version of CalEEMod (2022.1.1.14) to calculate both the construction
and operational emissions from the project site3. Project construction is modeled to commence no
earlier than September 2024 and be completed by August 2025. Construction assumes demolition,
grading, building construction, paving, and architectural coating. CalEEmod defaults were utilized.
Assumptions and output calculations are provided in Appendix C.

5.4  Localized Operational Emissions
Project-related air emissions from on-site sources such as architectural coatings, landscaping equipment,
on-site usage of natural gas appliances as well as the operation of vehicles on-site may have the potential
to exceed the State and Federal air quality standards in the project vicinity, even though these pollutant
emissions may not be significant enough to create a regional impact to the Air Basin. However, it should
be noted that the project would most likely not bring additional vehicle trips to the area due to the limits
on vehicles on Catalina Island. Trips would primarily be generated by taking workers and guests to and
from transportation to the island, such as a ferry, and would not occur on the island.

According to SCAQMD LST methodology, LSTs would apply to the operational phase of a project, if the
project includes stationary sources, or attracts mobile sources (such as heavy-duty trucks) that may spend
long periods queuing and idling at the site; such as industrial warehouse/transfer facilities. The proposed
project is a hotel and does not include such uses. Therefore, due to the lack of stationary source
emissions, no long-term localized significance threshold analysis is warranted.

5.6  Consistency with Applicable Plans

Consistency with the City’s General Plan

The project site is located in the City of Avalon. The project site has a current land use classification of
Special Commercial according to the City. The proposed project is a hotel. Therefore, the proposed
project is consistent with the land use and zoning designations of the City’s plans.

The project will be subject to the policies and ordinances pertaining to air quality in the City’s General
Plan. Project emissions have demonstrated that they will be below any significant thresholds as
outlined by SCAQMD.

6.0  Conclusions
Construction and operational project emissions were evaluated and compared to both regional and
localized SCAQMD’s thresholds of significance. Project emissions are anticipated to be below SCAQMD’s
thresholds of significance with no mitigation. Therefore, the impact is less than significant.

6.1. Climate Risk Summary
Cal-Adapt midcentury 2040–2059 average projections for four hazards are reported below for your project location. These are under Representation Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5 which assumes GHG
emissions will continue to rise strongly through 2050 and then plateau around 2100.
Climate Hazard  Result for Project Location  Unit

Temperature and Extreme Heat  —  annual days of extreme heat

Extreme Precipitation  —  annual days with precipitation above 20 mm

Sea Level Rise  —  meters of inundation depth

Wildfire  —  annual hectares burned

Temperature and Extreme Heat data are for grid cell in which your project are located. The projection is based on the 98th historical percentile of daily maximum/minimum temperatures from observed
historical data (32 climate model ensemble from Cal-Adapt, 2040–2059 average under RCP 8.5). Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.
Extreme Precipitation data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The threshold of 20 mm is equivalent to about ¾ an inch of rain, which would be light to moderate rainfall if received over a full
day or heavy rain if received over a period of 2 to 4 hours. Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.
Sea Level Rise data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The projections are from Radke et al. (2017), as reported in Cal-Adapt (Radke et al., 2017, CEC-500-2017-008), and consider
inundation location and depth for the San Francisco Bay, the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta and California coast resulting different increments of sea level rise coupled with extreme storm events.
Users may select from four scenarios to view the range in potential inundation depth for the grid cell. The four scenarios are: No rise, 0.5 meter, 1.0 meter, 1.41 meters
Wildfire data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The projections are from UC Davis, as reported in Cal-Adapt (2040–2059 average under RCP 8.5), and consider historical data of climate,
vegetation, population density, and large (> 400 ha) fire history. Users may select from four model simulations to view the range in potential wildfire probabilities for the grid cell. The four simulations make
different assumptions about expected rainfall and temperature are: Warmer/drier (HadGEM2-ES), Cooler/wetter (CNRM-CM5), Average conditions (CanESM2), Range of different rainfall and temperature
possibilities (MIROC5). Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.

Introduction
Executive Summary and Project Location
Environmental Science Associates (ESA) was retained by Christopherhill Development, Inc. to
prepare a Historic Resources Assessment Report (Report) for the building located at 301 Beacon
Street, Avalon, Catalina Island (Subject Property). The Subject Property is located on Lot 53,
Block 22, assessor parcel number 7480-031-040 within the City of Avalon, as shown in Figure 1,
Regional and Project Vicinity Map. The parcel is currently developed with a multi-family
apartment building constructed in 1923, as shown in Figure 2, Aerial Map. The project site is
situated on a steep hill in the southwest part of Avalon, at the southeast corner of Metropole
Avenue and Beacon Street. The building is in a vernacular style although elements of the
Mediterranean style are evident.

The Subject Property was evaluated in this Report for the potential eligibility for listing on the
National Register of Historic Places (National Register) and the California Register of Historical
Resources (California Register). The Report includes a discussion of the survey methods used, an
overview of the history of the surrounding area, and a description and evaluation of the Subject
Property. Through research, survey, and subsequent evaluation under the applicable Federal and
State eligibility criteria, ESA finds that the 301 Beacon Street does not retain historical or
architectural significance and should be assigned a code 6Z meaning it is ineligible for National
Register, California Register or Local designation through survey evaluation.

Regulatory Framework
Historical resources fall within the jurisdiction of the Federal, State, and Local designation
programs. Federal laws provide the framework for the identification of historical resources, and
in certain instances, protection. State and Local jurisdictions play active roles in the identification,
documentation, and protection of such resources within their communities. The National Historic
Preservation Act (NHPA) of 1966, as amended, and the California Public Resources Code (PRC),
Section 5024.1, are the primary Federal and State laws governing the evaluation and significance
of historical resources of national, state, regional, and local importance in the state of California.

 Federal Eligibility Criteria and Integrity Aspects
National Register of Historic Places
The National Register was established by the NHPA as “an authoritative guide to be used by
Federal, State, and Local governments, private groups and citizens to identify the Nation’s
cultural resources and to indicate what properties should be considered for protection from
destruction or impairment.” 1 The National Register recognizes properties that are significant at
the national, state, and/or local levels.

To be eligible for listing in the National Register, a resource must be significant in American
history, architecture, archaeology, engineering, or culture. Four criteria for evaluation have been
established to determine the significance of a resource. They include the following:
  Criterion A. Associated with events that have made a significant contribution to the broad
  patterns of our history;

  Criterion B. Associated with the lives of persons significant in our past;

  Criterion C. Embodies the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, or method of construction
  or that represent the work of a master, or that possess high artistic values, or that represent a
  significant and distinguishable entity whose components may lack individual distinction;

  Criterion D. Yields, or may be likely to yield, information important in prehistory or
  history. 2

Districts, sites, buildings, structures, and objects that are 50 years in age or older must meet one
or more of the above criteria and retain integrity of location, design, setting, materials,
workmanship, feeling, and association to be eligible for listing.

Within the concept of integrity, the National Register recognizes seven aspects or qualities that, in
various combinations, define integrity: Location, Design, Setting, Materials, Workmanship,
Feeling, and Association:

Location is the place where the historic property was constructed or the place where the historic
event occurred. The relationship between the property and its location is often important to
understanding why the property was created or why something happened. The actual location of a
historic property, complemented by its setting, is particularly important in recapturing the sense
of historic events and persons. Except in rare cases, the relationship between a property and its
historic associations is destroyed if the property is moved.

Design is the combination of elements that create the form, plan, space, structure, and style of a
property. It results from conscious decisions made during the original conception and planning of
a property (or its significant alteration) and applies to activities as diverse as community
planning, engineering, architecture, and landscape architecture. Design includes such elements as

 organization of space, proportion, scale, technology, ornamentation, and materials. A property’s
design reflects historic functions and technologies, as well as aesthetics. It includes such
considerations as the structural system; massing; arrangement of spaces; pattern of fenestration;
textures and colors of surface materials; type, amount and style of ornamental detailing; and
arrangement and type of plantings in a designed landscape.

Setting is the physical environment of a historic property. Whereas location refers to the specific
place where a property was built or an event occurred, setting refers to the character of the place
in which the property played its historic role. It involves how, not just where, the property is
situated and its relationship to surrounding features and open space.

Workmanship is the physical evidence of the crafts of a particular culture or people during any
given period in history or prehistory. It is the evidence of artisans’ labor and skill in constructing
or altering a building, structure, object, or site. Workmanship can apply to the property as a whole
or to its individual components.

Materials are the physical elements that were combined or deposited during a particular period of
time and in a particular pattern or configuration to form a historic property.

The choice and combination of materials reveal the preferences of those who created the property
and indicate the availability of particular types of materials and technologies. A property must
retain key exterior materials dating from the period of its historic significance.

Feeling is a property’s expression of the aesthetic or historic sense of a particular period of time.
It results from the presence of physical features that, taken together, convey the property’s
historic character.

Association is the direct link between an important historic event or person and a historic
property. A property retains association if it is the place where the event or activity occurred and
is sufficiently intact to convey that relationship to an observer. 3

To retain historic integrity, a property will always possess most of the aspects described above.
Depending upon its significance, retention of specific aspects of integrity may be paramount for a
property to convey its significance. 4 Determining which of these aspects are most important to a
particular property requires knowing why, where and when a property is significant. 5 For properties
that are considered significant under National Register Criteria A and B, National Register Bulletin
15: How to Apply the National Register Criteria for Evaluation (National Register Bulletin 15)
explains, “a property that is significant for its historic association is eligible if it retains the essential
physical features that made up its character or appearance during the period of its association with
the important event, historical pattern, or person(s).” 6 In assessing the integrity of properties that are

State Register and Eligibility Criteria
California Register of Historical Resources
The California Register was created by Assembly Bill 2881 which was signed into law on
September 27, 1992. The California Register is “an authoritative listing and guide to be used by
state and local agencies, private groups, and citizens in identifying the existing historical
resources of the state and to indicate which resources deserve to be protected, to the extent
prudent and feasible, from substantial adverse change.” 9 The criteria for eligibility for the
California Register are based upon National Register criteria. 10

The California Register consists of resources that are listed automatically and those that must be
nominated through an application and public hearing process. The California Register
automatically includes the following:
•  California properties listed on the National Register and those formally Determined Eligible
  for the National Register; 11
•  California Registered Historical Landmarks from No. 770 onward;
•  Those California Points of Historical Interest (PHI) that have been evaluated by the OHP and
  have been recommended to the State Historical Commission for inclusion on the California
  Register. 12

Other resources which may be nominated to the California Register include:
•  Individual historical resources;
•  Historical resources contributing to historic districts;
•  Historical resources identified as significant in historical resources surveys with significance
  ratings of Category 1 through 5;

To be eligible for the California Register, a historical resource must be significant at the local,
state, or national level, under one or more of the following four criteria:
1. Is associated with events that have made a significant contribution to the broad patterns of
  California’s history and cultural heritage;
2. Is associated with the lives of persons important in our past;

  or represents the work of an important creative individual, or possesses high artistic values; or
4. Has yielded, or may be likely to yield, information important in prehistory or history.

Additionally, a historical resource eligible for listing in the California Register must meet one or
more of the criteria of significance described above and retain enough of its historic character or
appearance to be recognizable as a historical resource and to convey the reasons for its significance.
Historical resources that have been rehabilitated or restored may be evaluated for listing. Integrity is
evaluated with regard to the retention of seven aspects of integrity similar to the National Register
(location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, feeling, and association). Also like the National
Register, it must be judged in context to the particular criteria under which a resource is proposed
for eligibility. Alterations over time to a resource or historic changes in its use may themselves have
historical, cultural, or architectural significance.

Also implemented at the state level, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires
projects to identify any substantial adverse impacts which may affect the significance of
identified historical resources.

The project site is in the City of Avalon on Catalina Island. A brief history of Catalina Island, and

Catalina Island and the Development of Avalon
The history of Catalina Island and the Development of Avalon below was adapted from Jeanine
L. Pederson’s Images of America, Catalina Island unless otherwise noted.

Catalina Island was first discovered by the Spanish explorer Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo, around
1542. Native Americans who had occupied the land for thousands of years were removed from
the island to the San Gabriel Mission and other parts of Los Angeles in the 1820s. In 1846,
Governor Pio Pico awarded Catalina Island to Thomas Robbins, a sea captain. Jose Maria
Covarrubias purchased “Rancho Santa Catalina” in 1850, and later sold it to Albert Packard in
1853. By 1864, James Lick, an American real estate investor owned the island in its entirety.

In 1887, developer and entrepreneur George Shatto of Grand Rapids, Michigan, purchased
Catalina Island to develop into a pleasure resort and to lease a portion of the land to miners and
ranchers. Shatto spent thousands of dollars on surveys, plans, and island maps and brought his
wife’s brother Edwin to the island to assume a supervisor role for major construction projects. 17
After the initial planning, streets were laid out, and lots were auctioned to the public by his
partner Charles A. Sumner, who operated the C.A. Sumner & Co. real estate agent on the island.
The public auction involved two steamships chartered by Shatto to bring potential buyers to the
island for lots that ranged in price from $75 to $1,800. The town was named Avalon, a word of
Celtic origin meaning “Island of Apples,” after Edwin Whitney’s wife, Etta Marilla, decided the
name appropriately depicted the island’s beauty. Once complete, the Hotel Metropole was the
main lodging available for tourists, but designated lots around the city allowed visitors to pitch
tents for an affordable lodging option. Tents for tourists became so popular that Avalon got the
nickname of “Rag City.” 18 Permanent dwellings were also constructed throughout the city,

 including the Whitney house (Edwin and Etta), 1888, and the Holly Hill House, constructed by
Peter Gano from 1889 to 1890. 19

In 1891, Shatto defaulted on his loans and was forced to sell the island to William, Hancock, and
Joseph Brent Banning, the sons of Phineas, who was in the transportation business and helped
develop Wilmington, California. The Banning brothers owned and operated the Wilmington
Transportation Company and continued Shatto’s vision of making Avalon a thriving resort
community. One of their significant contributions to the development of Avalon was a fleet of
steamships that provided increased access to the island and was coordinated with the Pacific
Electric Railroad schedule on the mainland. The Banning brothers, through their company, the
Banning Company, also constructed a dance hall, aquarium, and bath house, and expanded the
Hotel Metropole. Avalon’s “Rag City” continued during the Banning-era with rows of tents laid
out across multiple blocks of the city with frame floors and canvas sides. These could be rented
for $7.50 per week including bedding, furnishings, and basic cooking amenities. The second hotel
in Avalon, the Glenmore Hotel, was constructed in 1891 on Sumner Avenue by the same builders
who constructed the Hotel del Coronado in San Diego and was owned and operated by the
Whitney family. 20 It experienced fires and remodels over the years but is extant today as the
oldest hotel on the island.

In October 1894, the Banning Brothers established the Santa Catalina Island Company and hoped
to model Avalon as a type of “Company Town,” for permanent residents providing services such
as water, electricity, and gas without passing these costs down to the residents. 21 This
arrangement later caused issues between the company and residents and the Freeholders
Improvement Association was established by the boatman and homeowners to protect their
interests. The Avalon Inn, another popular lodging accommodation, was constructed in 1896 by
Mrs. E. Allen and located on Beacon Street. The first school was also established in 1896 to serve
the permanent residents and their children. In November of 1915, a devastating fire burned half of
Avalon’s buildings, including six hotels and several clubs. Homes from Whittley Avenue to Hill
Street were destroyed and residents were left homeless.

This fire eventually resulted in a huge debt for the Banning family, and combined with World
War I’s negative effect on tourism, they were forced to sell the island in 1919. William Wrigley,
Jr., a chewing gum magnate from Chicago and a seasonal resident of Pasadena, purchased the
island when he took control of the Santa Catalina Island Company between 1919 through 1932.
By 1921, Mr. Wrigley had completed his Avalon residence, named “Mt. Ada,” located on a high
hill overlooking the Pacific Ocean. Throughout the remainder of the decade, Mr. Wrigley and his
wife, Ada Foote Wrigley, implemented a large‐scale vision to reinvent Catalina Island as a
premier resort destination through a comprehensive program of civic improvements and tourist
attractions. These improvements included tourist lodging (Hotel Atwater), numerous attractions

 (Bird Park, Avalon Casino, and an expanded golf course), picturesque landscape elements

Tile and Pottery Plant. Mr. Wrigley also developed the Island’s infrastructure to facilitate tourist
travel, which included submarine cables for improved communications with the mainland and
new steamships, such as the S.S. Avalon and the S.S. Catalina. In addition to Wrigley’s numerous
physical improvements, the island supported many leisure activities for visitors, including golf
tournaments, sport competitions, marlin angling, and entertainment by the era’s top performers at
the Avalon Casino. As owner of the Chicago Cubs, Mr. Wrigley located the team’s spring
training practice on Catalina Island in 1921. Except during World War II, the team held their

The improvements that Wrigley, Jr. implemented on the island soon attracted visitors and
Catalina became synonymous with entertainment and play. By the late 1920s, over 400,000
tourists visited Catalina Island annually. Hollywood filmmakers also flocked to the island,
utilizing its diverse landscapes as set locations. On film, the island represented a wide range of
destinations, including Tahiti, Africa, and the American West. Many of the era’s most prominent
actors and movie industry celebrities, like Charlie Chaplin, Cecil B. DeMille, Dolores Del Rio,
Jean Harlow, Errol Flynn and Clark Gable worked and played on Catalina Island during the
1920s and 1930s. 23 Wrigley passed away in 1932 and his ownership of the island was passed to
his son Philip K. Wrigley. Catalina remains a popular tourism destination to the present day, with
numerous hotels, restaurants, shops, and a variety of watersport activities.

As described above, in 1919, William Wrigley Jr. acquired the island which resulted in the
continuation of Shatto and the Banning brother’s efforts to develop Avalon into a resort town.
Tract 3368, inclusive of the Subject Property and many of the surrounding blocks, was platted the
same year by the Santa Catalina Island Company. During this period, guidebooks and newspaper
articles advertised numerous options for visitor lodging including hotels, apartments, tents, and
bungalows. Sanborn maps from 1919 show a large building labeled “Lodging” at 225 Beacon
Street, to the west of the future Subject Property. 39 The rest of the block continued to contain
apartments and flats on Metropole Avenue, along with some permanent dwellings and tents on
some of the parcels. City Hall and a fire department were constructed on Metropole Avenue to
the northeast of the Subject Property by 1919.

Into the 1920s, rows of bungalows can be seen on Claressa Avenue and Descanso Avenue north
of Beacon Street. The Santa Catalina Island advertised these bungalows as short-term rentals for
$25.00 to $35.00 per month (Figure 10). 40 The Santa Catalina Island Company took over the
management of the Island Villa tents, which was advertised as an “open air hotel” in the 1920s. 41
It is unclear who commissioned the Subject Property, the White House Apartments, constructed
in 1923, but this was during a time in which the island was rapidly developing as a tourist haven
and profit was a likely motivation. The island received much press and investment during the
Wrigley years, and the White House Apartments would have helped fill the demand of tourists
and seasonal visitors to Catalina Island.

In 1942, the United States Maritime Service troops were stationed at Catalina Island. The Hotel
Atwater, Hotel St. Catherine, Island Villa, and other buildings were leased to the Maritime
Service for troops’ lodging, reflective of a slump in island tourism during the war years. In the
years that followed the end of World War II, a playful souvenir map from 1947 depicted the
Island Villa still in existence near the Subject Property, and the Chicago Cubs field to the west of
Beacon Street, which was constructed by Wrigley for spring training. The map also depicts that
the Catalina Hospital, a jeweler, and the United Airlines office are situated near the Subject
Property on Sumner Avenue and Metropole Avenue (Figure 11). 42

The neighborhood today remains a mixture of a few early buildings constructed in the first
decade of the1900s and Wrigley-era construction. The Subject Property is one of a handful of
examples of an early 20th century multi-family property in the neighborhood and within Avalon.

Lot Development
Lot 53, Block 22 (Subject Property)
Sanborn maps were used to determine the development of the Subject Property at 301 Beacon
Street. The first Sanborn map from 1894 depicts an empty lot with a tent with a frame floor
located on the east of the lot (Figure 12). The block at this time had been unofficially divided
into rectangular lots oriented towards Beacon Street, although this changed later with the official
subdivision of the lots. By 1898, one large corner lot on Metropole Avenue and Beacon Street
was shown on the Sanborn map. A narrow rectangular frame building on the eastern portion of
the subject lot that fronted onto Beacon Street was labeled as the Avalon Inn (Figure 13). Five
tents with frame floors were situated at the rear and front of the lot with one of the tents on the
site of the future subject parcel. The addresses associated with the large lot, inclusive of the future
subject parcel were originally 42-46 Beacon Street. By 1902, the Sanborn map depicted the large
lot still containing the Avalon Inn, and the two tents fronting Beacon Street were labeled as frame
structures with “part canvas sides,” and two tents are located at the rear of the lot (Figure 14).
The Sanborn map from 1909 depicted little change to the large lot.

As mentioned above in the Neighborhood Development, Tract 3368, inclusive of the Subject
Property, was platted in 1919 by the Santa Catalina Island Company. By 1919, the Avalon Inn on
the Sanborn map simply read “Lodgings” and a few other frame dwellings existed on the lot at
305 and 303 Beacon Street (Figure 15). The Subject Property was constructed in 1923 on the
north corner of the large lot, as illustrated in the 1924 Sanborn map, and was soon listed as the
White House Apartments in city directories (Figure 16). It appears the rectilinear dwelling at 303
Beacon Street was demolished to construct the Subject Property. As detailed in the construction
history below, no builder information for the original construction was located.

Architectural Description
The property located at 301 Beacon Street is situated on the southeast corner of Beacon Street and
Metropole Avenue. The parcel contains a 5,882 square-foot multi-family apartment house with 11
units. The property is built to the edge of the lot and is slightly graded to conform to the relatively
steep hill it sits on, which slopes up toward the southwest. The property extends across most of
the lot and a small rear yard at the southwest is enclosed with a lattice gate and wooden fence.
Designed in a vernacular style, with elements of Mediterranean Revival, the Subject Property was
constructed in 1923. The rectangular plan includes two shallow wings that project from the east
and south corners. The three-story property includes a flat roof that has a centralized stepped
parapet at the northwest elevation. The stepped parapet meets in the center of the northwest
elevation and includes a tower-like projection with a hipped roof that extends beyond the
roofline. The main roof appears to be clad in rolled asphalt and the tower is clad in shingles. The
building is of wood frame construction, sheathed in non-original vinyl siding. Limited horizontal
wood clapboard siding remains underneath the replacement siding, although it is unlikely to be
original.

There are recessed ground-level entrances at all four elevations, framed by archways and
accessed by concrete steps with original wood landings. All doors except one are wooden with
multi-pane glazing. The door appears to be from the original construction date of 1923 and
consists of three panels and one lite. The northeast elevation contains recessed entrances framed
by archways that lead to a metal fire escape on the upper levels. There is an upper-level door
surmounted by a pent roof on the southwest elevation that used to contain a balcony or external
stairway that has been removed. The entrance on the southeast elevation is surmounted by a metal
canopy (likely not original). Fenestration appears to be original consisting of double-hung, one
over one wood frame windows with lamb’s tongue details. The first-floor windows on all
elevations are covered with wooden lattices that may be original. No decorative detailing exists
on the vernacular structure (Figures 17-29).

Historic Context
The Subject Property at 301 Beacon Street was evaluated within the context of the city of Avalon,
within Tract 3368. ESA evaluated the Subject Property against the criteria for listing in the
National Register, California Register, and as a local resource. The historic context for the multi-
family apartment houses, Vernacular Architecture, and the Mediterranean Revival Style provided
the background and guidelines necessary to evaluate the architectural significance of 301 Beacon
Street. The period of significance associated with the Subject Property is its construction date of
1923.

Apartment Houses (1895-1970)
The Subject Property is an example of a multi-family housing constructed during an early period
of development in Avalon, shortly after Wrigley purchased Catalina Island. Excerpts from the

  The apartment house can best be defined in contrast to the bungalow court and other
  forms of courtyard housing that were being constructed in the early twentieth century.
  Unlike courtyard housing, the apartment house is designed to maximize lot coverage,
  with little or no lot area land dedicated to useable open space. And unlike courtyard
  housing, which is typically oriented onto a central common space, apartment houses are
  oriented toward the street, with architectural detailing concentrated on the street-facing
  façade. Apartment houses vary widely in terms of density, from one-story duplexes to
  high-rise luxury apartment towers. They can accommodate a variety of architectural
  styles, and therefore often reflect the dominant residential styles of the period in which
  they were constructed. 63

  One of the earliest and most modest types of apartment housing in Los Angeles was the
  duplex. There were several reasons that development of the duplex prevailed during the
  early days of multi-family development in the city. Chief among them was the fact that
  duplexes presented even the average homeowner with the opportunity to capitalize on the
  concurrent population and real estate booms. Composed of two separate dwelling units,
  the arrangement of the typical duplex allowed the homeowner to live in one unit while
  renting out the other, thus enabling the construction of both a residence and income
  property on a single lot. Duplexes were also appealing because their size and scale
  resembled that of the single-family homes with which they sometimes shared the block.
  The similarity in scale and massing allowed duplexes to be designed in many of the same
  styles as were popular for single-family residences at the time, including the Craftsman
  style and various Period Revival styles. 64

  Apartment houses of all sizes grew in popularity as developers sought higher-density
  solutions to the population boom. Some were smaller, typically two stories in height, with
  three or four units. Like duplexes, they were designed in the prevailing architectural
  styles of day. Larger apartment houses from this early period could range anywhere from
  two to six stories in height, with four or more units. Early examples constructed during
  the 1910s were mostly modest vernacular structures constructed of brick or wood frame,
  while into the 1920s they began to take on more decorative, even fanciful, stylistic
  elements. Their comparative affordability and the ability to pack as many units onto a lot
  as possible made the two-story apartment building a particularly attractive investment for

Vernacular Architecture
As mentioned above, the Subject Property is an example of vernacular architecture for an
apartment house from 1923. A brief description of vernacular architecture from the Los Angeles
Citywide Historic Context Statement, Architecture and Engineering/Late 19th and Early 20th
Century Residential Architecture was used to establish the evaluation for the Subject Property
under this style. 67 The Subject Property’s vernacular design also contains a modest influence of
the Mediterranean Revival Style, as detailed in the following architectural context. The character-
defining features of the Subject Property include minimal detailing, a simple plan, and
construction by a local builder. Visual inspection during ESA’s site visit yielded only a few
vernacular style examples throughout Avalon, as most were lost in the 1915 fire, or altered over
time. It also revealed that the stepped parapet motif seen on the Subject Property is popular on
other properties in Avalon, particularly single-family houses. As was common with builders, they
also mixed vernacular style with elements of Craftsman or Mediterranean Revival. The Subject
Property does not contain design elements of Folk Victorian as described in the SurveyLA
context below, however the vernacular style described below can be translated to the design of

  Several styles from this period of development in Los Angeles are best classified as
  vernacular architecture. According to historian Alan Gowans, “vernacular architecture is
  the use of architectural style without being conscious of style.” 68 Nevertheless, even the
  minimal design features of vernacular buildings were often influenced by nationwide
  stylistic trends that emerged during this particularly transitional era. It was only through
  technological advances that many of the earlier high-style forms were simplified for mass
  production to meet the needs of various socio-economic classes and thus took on
  vernacular forms. The Folk Victorian style, for example, was largely the product of the
  Industrial Revolution. The style was doubtlessly influenced by Queen Anne and Eastlake
  with bold ornamentation in the form of pre-cut wooden scrollwork, spindle work, and
  trim, yet are easily distinguishable by their small scale and simple rectangular or L-
  shaped plans. With the invention of improved, mechanized woodworking tools and the
  expansion of the railroads, even relatively modest homes could feature elaborate

Mediterranean Revival Style (1887-1942)
The Subject Property is vernacular in style although it contains a few elements of Italian
influence as part of the Mediterranean Revival style of 1887-1942. 69 The modest elements of the
style include the massing with two projecting wings, the stacked archways, and the low hipped
roof tower on the northwest elevation. The St. Catherine Hotel, and Tuna Club are both high-style
examples in Avalon that may have served as inspiration for the Subject Property. The St.
Catherine Hotel was constructed on Catalina Island from 1917 to 1918, and the Tuna Club was
constructed earlier in 1916. It is not clear if the builder for 301 Beacon Street drew inspiration
from this impressive hotel or the highly visible Tuna Club, or just the style in general. Elements
can also be seen in the old schoolhouse which was torn down in 1930, such as the hipped roof
tower and arches. Although the Subject Property only contains modest elements of the style, a
brief context for the Mediterranean Style is included below.

Mediterranean Revival architecture (sometimes called Italian Renaissance) is a style that was
used in early 20th century residential architect across the United States, especially after World
War I. The style emerged in the late 19th century when it was primarily used for high-style
residences designed by professional architects for wealthy clients. The well-known architecture
firm of McKim, Mead & White is credited with sparking the revival with the Villard Houses in
New York. As opposed to its predecessor, the Italianate style, the Mediterranean Revival or
Italian Renaissance style more closely evoked examples of Italian domestic architecture. This was
primarily due to the fact that increased mobility between America and Europe had allowed many
architects and their clients to visit Italy, giving them firsthand knowledge of the country’s
architecture. Additionally, advances in masonry veneering in the early 20th century allowed for
better imitation of the stone and stucco that typically clad the original Italian buildings that
inspired the American designs. These new techniques also helped the style to spread to more
vernacular uses as the style came within the financial means of the middle-class in the 1920s. The
style began to decline in the 1930s and had virtually disappeared from use by World War II
(Figures 30-32).

The typical character-defining feature of this style are a low-pitched hipped roof, wide
overhanging eaves with decorative brackets, ceramic tile roof, smaller and less elaborate upper
story windows, round arches above doors or first story windows, entrance accented by classical
columns or pilasters, and a symmetrical façade. The exterior walls are typically clad in stone,
stucco, or brick. Common decorative details include quoins, roof-line balustrades, pedimented

 Significance Evaluation
ESA reviewed the dwelling located on the Subject Property for significance under the federal,
state, and city criteria as outlined below.

Broad Patterns of History
With regard to broad patterns of history, the following are the relevant criteria:

•  National Register Criterion A: Is associated with events that have made a significant
  contribution to the broad patterns of our history.
•  California Register Criterion 1: Is associated with events that have made a significant
  contribution to the broad patterns of California's history and cultural heritage.

The Subject Property was built in 1923 in the southwest portion of Avalon, Catalina on a steep
hill by an unknown builder and owner. While records could not be located to confirm exact dates,
Joseph Cameron may have purchased the building shortly after it was constructed. He is shown to
have owned and be living there with his brother and his brother’s family, and renters in the 1930
census. Constructed as a 10-unit apartment, and listed in directories as the White House
Apartments, residents appear to be a mix of seasonal visitors and long-term residents of Avalon.
The earliest buildings in the neighborhood were the Congregational Church and the Avalon Inn
from the late 1800s. The neighborhood developed into a tourist area in the early 1900s through
the 1920s with a mixture of cottages, bungalows, and tent cities. Rooming houses and apartment
houses were constructed to meet the demand of the tourist industry and housed many of the
workers in the tourist industry and local stores. The Subject Property housed local workers in the
restaurant industries and other modest trades and does not appear to have been strongly associated
with the tourism industry of Catalina Island.

301 Beacon Street remains today as a modest example of an apartment house constructed in the
1920s, shortly after Wrigley acquired the island. The Subject Property appears to be a typical
multi-family apartment house constructed in Avalon as well as the larger context of Los Angeles
County and is not a unique development. While the building is representative of the increased
residential settlement patterns of Avalon during the 1920s, it is one of multiple properties from
the same period that remain extant in Avalon. The property does not appear to have influenced
any building trends for multi-family properties in Avalon and is not associated with events that
have made significant contributions to broad patterns of national, state and local history. While it
is a good example of a large multi-family apartment house in the community, it does not appear
to be significant or any trends or patterns of development in Avalon in the 1920s or since.

Therefore, 301 Beacon Street does not appear to meet the significance requirements as a
historical resource under National Register Criterion A and California Register Criterion 1.
No local criteria exist for the City of Avalon.

 Significant Persons
With regard to associations with important persons, the following are the relevant criteria:
•  National Register Criterion B: Is associated with the lives of persons significant in our past.
•  California Register Criterion 2: Is associated with the lives of persons important in our

As mentioned above, no builder or architect was found for 301 Beacon Street, but the Cameron
family appears to have acquired it sometime after it was built, likely around 1930. The Subject
Property is referred to as the “White House Apartments” in city directories, and housed members
of the Cameron family from circa 1930 to circa 2002. Three generations of the Cameron family
(Joseph, Michael, and Louis) were in the food and beverage industry, owning and operating bars
and restaurants in Avalon. Their involvement in local restaurants and bars was not found to be
significant to the local history of Avalon. While the Cameron family lived in Avalon for many
years, and is well-known among local residents, the family does not appear to have made
significant contributions to local, state or national history. In addition, no other occupants of the
Subject Property were found to be significant under Criterion B/2.

Therefore, 301 Beacon Street does not appear to be associated with significant personages
or events as is required under National Register Criterion B and California Register
Criterion 2. No local criteria exist for the City of Avalon.

Architecture
With regard to architecture, design, or construction, the following are the relevant criteria:
•  National Register Criterion C: Embodies the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, or
  method of construction or that represent the work of a master, or that possess high artistic
  values, or that represent a significant and distinguishable entity whose components may lack
  individual distinction.
•  California Register Criterion 3: Embodies the distinctive characteristics of a type, period,
  region, or method of construction, or represents the work of an important creative individual,
  or possesses high artistic values.
The Subject Property at 301 Beacon Street is a good example of a vernacular style multi-family
residential building that contains modest elements of the Mediterranean Revival style. Dating
from 1923, it was constructed as a 10-unit apartment house. No builder or architect information
was located. Some remaining character-defining features of the Subject Property include the
Italian Renaissance wing massing, a hipped roof tower, arched entryways, and double-hung 1/1
wood sash windows from the 1920s. The parapet may be original to the construction of the
Subject Property due to the vernacular trend of combining styles and using locally available
materials and finishes. A hipped roof tower is also present on the building and mimics other
buildings in Avalon including the Tuna Club. The siding is not original and covers the original
horizontal wood siding. No major changes appear to have been made to the footprint of the
property. While the Subject Property represents an extant multi-family property in a vernacular
style, it is not a good example of any style or building typology in Avalon. Since no information
was found about a builder or architect, it could not be found significant as the work of a master. It

•  National Register Criterion D: It yields, or may be likely to yield, information important in

•  California Register Criterion 4: Has yielded, or may be likely to yield, information

While most often applied to archaeological districts and sites, Criterion D/4 can also apply to
buildings, structures, and objects that contain important information. In order for these types of
properties to be eligible under Criterion D/4, they themselves must be, or must have been, the
principal source of the important information. The Subject Property does not appear to yield
significant information that would expand our current knowledge or theories of design, methods
of construction, operation, or other information that is not already known about the period in
which it was constructed, the method of construction, or the design. The building reflects
common building practices and materials of the 1920s, which have already been well
documented. Furthermore, 1920s multi-family residential architectural styles have been preserved
and are available for study. Therefore, the Subject Property does not meet the significance
requirements under National Register Criterion D and California Register Criterion 4.

Conclusion
As a result of ESA’s research and survey investigations and, through the application of the
Federal and State eligibility evaluation criteria, ESA determined 301 Beacon Street is not eligible
under Criterion A/1, B/1, C/3, or D/4. No local criteria exist for the City of Avalon. While the
building is representative of early residential development in 1920s Avalon, it is not a unique or
rare example from this period and is not eligible under Criterion A/1. The Cameron family who
owned the Subject Property for the majority of its usable life are not significant persons within
the history of Avalon, Catalina Island, or the larger Southern California landscape and it is
therefore not eligible under B/2. It is a good example of a vernacular multi-family dwelling with
elements of the Mediterranean Revival style, but it is not an excellent or rare example. Therefore,
it is not eligible under Criterion C/3. Therefore, it is ESA’s recommendation that the Subject
Property be considered not eligible for the National Register or California Register through
survey evaluation and assigned a code 6Z.

City of Los Angeles, Venice Coastal Zone Survey, Los Angeles County, CA. Architectural Historian. Valerie expanded on

1000-1018 N. Croft Avenue, Historic Resource Assessment, Los Angeles, CA. Architectural Historian. Valerie provided
research, wrote historical contexts, and compiled a Historic Resource Assessment for four multi-family properties in
Hollywood. One property was designed in a Mediterranean Style using a house stock plan from the local company
Bungalowcraft. Two of the properties are Spanish Colonial Revival duplexes constructed in the 1920s and 1930s. The
fourth property was designed in 1940 by a notable Los Angeles architect who became known for his unique window
treatment and Minimal Traditional designs. The four properties were found significant as early dwellings in the
Hollywood Scenic Tract under Criterion A, and as excellent examples of three different architectural styles applied multi-
family properties under Criterion C.
133 Vieudelou Avenue, Historic Resource Assessment, Catalina Island, CA. Architectural Historian. Valerie researched
the oldest house in Avalon, Catalina Island and compiled a Historic Resource Assessment. The house belonged to a
family who settled on the island during the early days of development into a resort town. The house is Folk Victorian style
and constructed in 1888. The property was found eligible for the National Register and California Register for its
significance under Criterion A, B, and C.
301 Beacon Street, Historic Resource Assessment, Catalina Island, CA. Architectural Historian. Valerie researched a
multi-family property on Beacon Street in Avalon, Catalina Island and compiled a Historic Resource Assessment. The
dwelling has been owned by the same family who constructed it in 1923. The style is vernacular with elements of
Italianate and Mediterranean Revival. It was called the White House Apartments and housed the original family and other
short-term guests visiting the island. The property was found eligible as a rare example of a multi-family property from
the 1920s in Avalon, Catalina Island.
West San Gabriel Valley, Historic Context Statement, Los Angeles County, CA. Architectural Historian. Valerie
authored the residential section of the West San Gabriel Historic Context Statement which involved extensive research,
and the development of architectural context narratives and residential resource registration requirements. Valerie
conducted an archival record search at the South Central Coastal Information Center (SCCIC) to determine the presence
of cultural resources in eight unincorporated study areas.
211 Emerald Bay, California Register Nomination, Orange County, CA. Architectural Historian. Valerie provided
architectural historian services which included research, the development of historical contexts, and the preparation of a
nomination for the California Register of Historical Resources for a property in Emerald Bay. 211 Emerald Bay is in a
planned coastal “garden suburb” that was developed beginning in 1929. The community was designed by renowned
landscape architect Mark Daniels and notable Pasadena architects such as Roland Coate and H. Palmer Sabin. The house
at 211 Emerald Bay contributed to the early development of the neighborhood and is one of the last remaining intact
examples of the Mediterranean Revival aesthetic developed by the architectural review board and original developer.
AGBU Manoogian-Demirdjian School Improvements, Categorical Exemption, Canoga Park, CA. Architectural
Historian. Valerie provided research, wrote historical contexts, conducted a site visit, and compiled a Department of
Parks and Recreation form 523 and Notice of Exemption for an Armenian-American school in Canoga Park. The school is
operated by the Armenian General Benevolent Union (AGBU), and the organization purchased the parcel in 1985. The

Columbia University, The Harlem Renaissance: Preservation, Spatial Encounter, and Anti-Racism, Harlem, NY.
Architectural Historian/Student. As a graduate student, Valerie contributed to a group research report that examined the
legacy of the Harlem Renaissance, its significance in anti-Black racism histories and its place-based associations. This

innovative community lens. The goal of the report was to instrumentalize the heritage of the Harlem Renaissance toward
anti-racism and social justice while also identifying and preserving key assets for the Black community.
